parts.partTitle: Broker vs Log: Where State Resides

beats.headline: Is your message broker actually a database?
beats.subline: RabbitMQ and Kafka aren't just pipes; they store state in fundamentally different ways.
beats.narration: Stop treating RabbitMQ and Kafka as identical message pipes. One is a smart post office that deletes mail after delivery, the other is an immutable ledger that keeps everything forever. Choosing wrong is a production disaster.

beats.title: State Ownership Models
beats.subtitle: Broker-managed vs. Consumer-managed

nodes.label: RabbitMQ
nodes.detail: Broker tracks delivery state and deletes on ack

nodes.label: Kafka
nodes.detail: Broker stores append-only log; consumers track offset

nodes.label: Impact
nodes.detail: Broker controls routing; Log enables replay

beats.narration: In RabbitMQ, the broker keeps the state. It routes messages and deletes them once acknowledged. In Kafka, the broker is a dumb, append-only log. The consumers track their own progress, which makes replay trivial.

beats.title: Read Semantics
beats.narration: RabbitMQ is destructive. Once you ack, the message is gone. Kafka is non-destructive. You just move your bookmark, allowing multiple independent services to read the same data at their own pace.

beats.title: The Kafka Offset Advantage

steps.explanation: Each group gets its own independent position in the log.
Only moves the pointer; data remains on disk for others.

beats.narration: Notice the groupId. Because Kafka stores the log, a new service can join tomorrow, set its groupId, and start reading from the beginning of time. RabbitMQ simply cannot do this without custom audit tables.

beats.title: Part 1 Summary
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Push vs Pull and the backpressure trap →
beats.narration: That is the storage model. In Part 2, we look at how RabbitMQ pushes data while Kafka waits for you to pull, and why that matters for your JVM heap.

beats.headline: Why your consumer is crashing with OOM.
beats.subline: The delivery model dictates how your service handles traffic spikes.
beats.narration: If your consumer is crashing with OutOfMemory errors, you are likely mismanaging backpressure. RabbitMQ pushes data at you, while Kafka lets you pull at your own speed. The difference is critical.

beats.title: Delivery Dynamics
beats.subtitle: Push (Broker-driven) vs Pull (Consumer-driven)

nodes.label: RabbitMQ Push
nodes.detail: Broker floods consumer until prefetch limit

beats.narration: RabbitMQ pushes messages as they arrive. If you don't set a prefetch limit, it will fill your memory until you crash. Kafka waits for you to poll, so if you are slow, the data just sits on the broker.

beats.title: RabbitMQ Prefetch Control
beats.code:
spring:
  rabbitmq:
    listener:
      simple:
        acknowledge-mode: manual
        prefetch: 20 # <--- The safety valve

steps.explanation: Limits unacknowledged messages to 20. Broker stops pushing until you ack.

beats.narration: The prefetch value is your safety valve. Setting it to 20 means the broker stops sending data once 20 messages are unacknowledged. Without this, your consumer is a sitting duck for a traffic spike.

beats.title: Kafka Pull Batching
beats.caption: Configuring poll behavior

lines.text: # If processing slows, poll() is called later

beats.narration: Kafka's pull model is inherently safer. If your database slows down, your consumer just calls poll less frequently. The broker doesn't care; it just holds the data on disk until you're ready.

beats.title: Part 2 Summary
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Ordering pitfalls and partition keys →
beats.narration: Push is for low latency, pull is for high throughput and safety. In Part 3, we dive into the nightmare of ordering guarantees and why partition keys are non-negotiable in Kafka.

beats.headline: Your messages are arriving out of order.
beats.subline: Ordering is easy in a single queue, but breaks instantly at scale.
beats.narration: Think your system is FIFO? Think again. As soon as you add a second consumer to a queue or partition, race conditions will destroy your data integrity. Here is how to keep it strict.

beats.title: Ordering Constraints
beats.narration: RabbitMQ ordering is fragile. If Consumer A takes longer than Consumer B, your sequence is gone. Kafka forces order by pinning keys to specific partitions, ensuring one consumer handles that entity's stream.

beats.title: Kafka Partition Keying

steps.explanation: The key determines the partition. Same key = same partition = strict order.

beats.narration: Always use a partition key. By passing orderId, Kafka hashes it to a specific partition. This guarantees that every update for that order is processed in exact sequence by a single consumer.

beats.title: The Scaling Trap
beats.caption: Why you shouldn't change partitions

lines.text: # Changing partition count breaks hash mapping
# Order is now lost across the topic

beats.narration: Careful. If you increase partitions on an active topic, the hash mapping changes. Suddenly, new events for an order go to a different partition than the old ones. Your ordering is now broken.

beats.title: Part 3 Summary
takeaways: Use partition keys to maintain sequence

beats.narration: Ordering is a design choice, not a configuration toggle. In Part 4, we wrap up with a decision matrix to pick the right tool for your specific architecture.

beats.headline: Stop over-engineering your infrastructure.
beats.subline: Use this decision matrix to pick the right tool every time.
beats.narration: Stop picking Kafka because it's cool. Stop picking RabbitMQ because it's old. Use the tool that matches your data lifecycle. Here is the final decision matrix.

beats.title: Decision Matrix
beats.narration: Need complex routing or per-message TTL? RabbitMQ. Need to replay events or feed multiple downstream services from one source? Kafka. It's really that simple.

beats.title: The 'When to Pick' Guide
beats.subtitle: Architecture decision tree
beats.narration: Don't force Kafka to be a task queue. It lacks per-message ack and priority logic. Don't force RabbitMQ to be an event store. It will explode your RAM. Use both where they belong.

beats.title: Final Pro-Tip
beats.caption: The most common mistake

lines.text: Using Kafka for per-item priority queues
Use RabbitMQ, or a workflow engine like Temporal

beats.narration: The biggest mistake? Treating Kafka like a priority queue. It isn't. If you need to jump the line, use RabbitMQ or a workflow engine. Kafka is for the stream, not the individual task.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
takeaways: Avoid using Kafka as a priority queue
